objectives: Define a stock universe as it was known on each date.

screens.title: Point in time
screens.prose: A **point-in-time** universe uses only data known on its date. The course's rule: on date $t$ a share is in if it is listed on $t$ and its average daily £ volume over the 60 trading days up to $t$ is at least £5m. widget.solution:
import pandas as pd

def universe_on(p, date, min_adv_gbp=5e6, window=60):
    date = pd.Timestamp(date)
    vol = daily_volume_gbp(p).loc[:date].tail(window)
    full = vol.count() == window              # 60 days of volume, all known by date
    ok = p["listed"].loc[date] & full & (vol.mean() >= min_adv_gbp)
    return sorted(ok.index[ok])

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

def make_panel(n_stocks=200, n_days=1260, seed=2310):
    """Seeded stand-in for a few years of daily data on a share universe."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    names = [f"S{i:03d}" for i in range(n_stocks)]
    dates = pd.bdate_range("2019-01-02", periods=n_days)
    sector = rng.integers(0, 5, n_stocks)
    beta = 0.6 + 0.8 * rng.random(n_stocks)
    mkt = 0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(n_days)
    sec = 0.005 * rng.standard_normal((n_days, 5))
    z_mu = rng.standard_normal((n_days, n_stocks))
    z_tr = rng.standard_normal((n_days, n_stocks))
    idio = 0.015 * rng.standard_normal((n_days, n_stocks))
    mu = np.zeros(n_stocks); u = np.zeros(n_stocks)
    ret = np.empty((n_days, n_stocks))
    k = 0.0004 * np.sqrt(1 - 0.995 ** 2)
    for t in range(n_days):
        mu = 0.995 * mu + k * z_mu[t]              # slow drift: momentum
        u_new = 0.8 * u + 0.006 * z_tr[t]          # transient part: reversal
        ret[t] = beta * mkt[t] + sec[t, sector] + mu + idio[t] + (u_new - u)
        u = u_new
    # listings and delistings: 10% list late, 10% die (last day -50% to -100%)
    listed = np.ones((n_days, n_stocks), bool)
    late = rng.choice(n_stocks, n_stocks // 10, replace=False)
    for j in late:
        listed[: rng.integers(60, n_days // 2), j] = False
    dead = rng.choice(np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n_stocks), late), n_stocks // 10, replace=False)
    for j in dead:
        d = rng.integers(n_days // 4, n_days - 20)
        ret[d, j] = np.log(1 - rng.uniform(0.5, 1.0) + 1e-4)
        listed[d + 1 :, j] = False
    ret = np.where(listed, ret, np.nan)
    simple = np.expm1(ret)
    # dividends: half the shares pay 0.5% a quarter; splits: 15 two-for-one
    div_yield = np.zeros((n_days, n_stocks))
    payers = rng.random(n_stocks) < 0.5
    div_yield[63::63, :] = np.where(payers, 0.005, 0.0)
    split = np.ones((n_days, n_stocks))
    for j in rng.choice(n_stocks, 15, replace=False):
        split[rng.integers(100, n_days - 100), j] = 2.0
    price_ret = (1 + np.nan_to_num(simple)) / (1 + div_yield) - 1
    start = rng.uniform(20, 200, n_stocks)
    adj_close = start * np.cumprod(1 + price_ret, axis=0)    # split-adjusted, no dividends
    later = np.cumprod(split[::-1], axis=0)[::-1]              # splits on or after each day
    raw_close = adj_close * np.vstack([later[1:], np.ones(n_stocks)])
    # spreads and volume: bigger names are cheaper to trade
    size = rng.lognormal(0, 1, n_stocks)
    half_spread_bp = np.clip(8 / np.sqrt(size), 1, 30)
    adv_gbp = 2e7 * size
    F = lambda a: pd.DataFrame(a, index=dates, columns=names)
    return {"ret": F(simple), "raw_close": F(np.where(listed, raw_close, np.nan)),
            "adj_close": F(np.where(listed, adj_close, np.nan)),
            "dividend": F(np.where(listed, div_yield * raw_close, 0.0)),
            "split": F(split), "listed": F(listed),
            "sector": pd.Series(sector, index=names), "beta": pd.Series(beta, index=names),
            "half_spread_bp": pd.Series(half_spread_bp, index=names),
            "adv_gbp": pd.Series(adv_gbp, index=names)}

def daily_volume_gbp(p):
    """Each day's £ volume: p["volume_gbp"] if the panel has one, else adv_gbp on every listed day."""
    vol = p["volume_gbp"] if "volume_gbp" in p else p["listed"] * p["adv_gbp"]
    return vol.where(p["listed"])

def toy_panel():
    """The hand panel of this lesson: 120 days, five shares, a daily £ volume."""
    dates = pd.bdate_range("2019-01-02", periods=120)
    listed = pd.DataFrame(True, index=dates, columns=list("ABCDE"))
    listed.iloc[:30, 2] = False      # C lists on row 30
    listed.iloc[100:, 3] = False     # D's last day is row 99
    vol = pd.DataFrame({"A": 8e6, "B": 3e6, "C": 10e6, "D": 20e6, "E": 2e6}, index=dates)
    vol.iloc[70:, 4] = 12.5e6        # E trades far more from row 70
    return {"listed": listed, "volume_gbp": vol.where(listed), "adv_gbp": vol.mean()}

def spy_panel(p, cut, value):
    """A copy of p with every volume after row cut set to value, and every share listed."""
    q = dict(p)
    q["listed"] = p["listed"].copy(); q["listed"].iloc[cut + 1:] = True
    q["volume_gbp"] = p["volume_gbp"].copy(); q["volume_gbp"].iloc[cut + 1:] = value
    return q

toy = toy_panel()

small = make_panel(30, 300, 5)

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use only rows up to `date`, require all 60 of them, and sort the names.

byKey.test-1: On 25 March 2019 no share has 60 days of volume yet. Require `vol.count() == window`.
byKey.test-6: D's last day was 21 May. On 22 May it is not listed, so it must drop out.
byKey.test-7: Your answer on 17 April changed when later volumes changed. Read only rows up to `date`.

explain.text: `loc[:date].tail(window)` keeps the 60 rows known on the date, so later data cannot reach the answer. The spies prove it: rewriting every later volume leaves 17 April alone. An empty list before 26 March is correct, not a bug.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: What you did on each date, as one rule. With $L_{i,t}$ true when share $i$ is listed on $t$ and $V_{i,s}$ its £ volume on day $s$: $$U_t = \Big\{\, i : L_{i,t} \text{ and } \frac{1}{60}\sum_{s=t-59}^{t} V_{i,s} \ge \text{£}5\text{m} \,\Big\}$$ Every input is dated $t$ or earlier.
screens.question: Which change to `universe_mask` breaks the rule's point-in-time property?

options.text: `vol.rolling(60, center=True).mean()`
`vol.rolling(20, min_periods=20).mean()`
options.why: A 20-day window is shorter, but it still ends on $t$. It is a different rule, not a leak.

options.why: A higher bar changes who is in. It still uses only past volume.

options.why: A longer history delays new listings. It never reads after $t$.

A centred window of 60 rows reaches about 30 rows ahead.
`center=True` puts $t$ in the middle of the window, so it reads the future.

feedback.correct: A centred window reads about 30 days ahead.

screens.title: The vendor's file
screens.prose: A data vendor sells a file of an index's current members and their price histories since 2010. A team runs a momentum study on it and reports a strong long side. You review the study before it goes to the investment committee.
screens.question: Which questions should you ask about the universe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Was membership on each date decided from data known on that date?
Are shares that delisted during the study in the data, with their last returns?
Is there a liquidity filter, computed from trailing volume?
Which share had the best return over the study?
options.why: That describes the result. It says nothing about whether the universe was fair.

options.text: Is today's list fine if the study covers only the last two years?
options.why: Two years is shorter, but today's members are still the survivors of those two years.

hints.text: A universe can fail in three ways: dates, deaths and trading costs.
This file holds only today's members.
Ask about point-in-time membership, delisted shares and a trailing liquidity filter.

feedback.correct: Point in time, the dead, and liquidity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the questions about how the list of names was built.

byKey.best: The best share is a result. Ask how the list was built.
byKey.recent: A shorter study still uses today's survivors.

explain.text: Today's members include shares that joined because they rose, so momentum's long side looks better than it was. Delisted shares are absent, so losses vanish. Without a trailing liquidity filter, the study may trade shares nobody could trade at size.

ideas: A universe is rebuilt on every date from data known on that date: listed then, liquid then.
The course's rule: listed on $t$ and a trailing 60-day average £ volume of at least £5m. The first 59 days have no universe.
Today's list, however carefully dated, is a list of survivors and winners chosen with hindsight.

formula.name: Point-in-time universe
formula.note: Every input is dated $t$ or earlier.

summary.trap: Building the study from today's constituents. Dating each share from its listing does not bring back the shares that died.

quiz.prose: Edge case. A new panel starts on 1 March 2021, and the universe rule needs 60 trading days of volume, today included.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first day with 60 days of volume, that day included.

quiz.prose: A filter keeps shares whose average daily volume over 2019 to 2023 is at least £5m, and applies it on every date.
quiz.question: What is wrong with it?

options.text: On 2019 dates it uses volume from 2020 to 2023, which was not known then
Nothing: an average over five years is more stable than 60 days
options.why: Stable, but built from future data. On a 2019 date, 2023's volume is not yet known.

options.text: £5m is too low a threshold for a five-year average
options.why: The threshold is a choice. The fault is which days the average uses.

options.text: It drops dead shares
options.why: It may keep or drop them. The fault is that every date sees the whole period's volume.

feedback.correct: A whole-sample average leaks the future into every early date.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which days' volume a 2019 date may use.

explain.text: A share that became liquid in 2022 passes the filter in 2019 as well. The study then trades it when it was thin and costly. A trailing window uses only days up to each date.

quiz.prose: A share lists on Monday 4 March and trades £40m a day from its first day.

options.text: On its 60th trading day
On 4 March: its volume is far above £5m
options.why: One day of £40m is not a 60-day average. The rule waits for 60 days.

options.text: Never: shares that list during a study are left out
options.why: A new listing is investable once it passes the rule. Leaving it out is a choice made with hindsight.

options.text: After one year of trading
options.why: The course's rule needs 60 trading days, about three months.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The rule needs a 60-day average.

explain.text: Its 60-day average exists from its 60th day, and at £40m it passes then. Before that, it is listed but not yet judged.
